title: Rules of Inference and Argument Validity
quickIdea: An argument is valid when the premises cannot all be true while the conclusion is false. A short list of inference rules covers almost every GATE argument question.
remember: Argument form: premises above the line, conclusion below. It is valid when (premise1 and ... and premisen) -> conclusion is a tautology.
Modus ponens: p, p -> q, therefore q. Modus tollens: not q, p -> q, therefore not p.
Hypothetical syllogism: p -> q, q -> r, therefore p -> r.
Disjunctive syllogism: p or q, not p, therefore q. Addition: p, therefore p or q. Simplification: p and q, therefore p.
Resolution: p or r, q or not r, therefore p or q.
Fastest test: make the conclusion false, then try to satisfy every premise. If you cannot, the argument is valid.
Two named fallacies: affirming the consequent (p -> q, q, therefore p) and denying the antecedent (p -> q, not p, therefore not q). Both are invalid.

example.prompt: Premises: if it rains the match is not played; it rains. What follows, and is the argument valid?
example.work: R = it rains, P = the match is played. Premises are R -> not P and R; the conclusion not P follows by modus ponens. Making not P false forces P true, and then R -> not P is false while R is true, so no model makes the premises true and the conclusion false.
example.answer: Conclusion: the match is not played. The argument is valid.

gateAngle: GATE 2015 Set 2 Q.3 gives two statements and asks what follows by sound inference: from C -> not E and K -> E, the contrapositive E -> not C chains with K -> E to give K -> not C. The answer is the statement 'if a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt'.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Premises: p -> q and not q. What follows?
variations.why: If p were true, modus ponens would give q, contradicting not q. So p must be false. This is the contrapositive of the premise applied to not q.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Name the fallacy in: p -> q, q, therefore p.
variations.why: The row p = false, q = true makes both premises true and the conclusion false, so the argument has a counterexample model and is invalid.

trap.what: Using the converse of a premise as if it were the premise.
trap.why: p -> q allows q to be true while p is false. Anything that assumes q forces p is an invalid step.
trap.counterexample: From 'if a candidate is corrupt then he is not elected' and 'this candidate was not elected' you cannot conclude he is corrupt - he may simply have lost.

check.question: Which rule turns 'p or q' and 'not p' into 'q'?
check.explanation: One disjunct is ruled out, so the other must hold. It is valid in every row where both premises are true.
